newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria co-op bank raises capital to 15 bln levs.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria co-op bank raises capital to 15 bln levs.

text.p: Bulgaria's Central Co-operative Bank (CCB) would raise its capital to 15 billion levs from two billion levs through a new share issue, a CCB executive director said.

"The shareholders decided to raise capital to 15 billion levs. After the increase 14.850 billion levs will be in voting shares and 150 million levs will be in non-voting ones," Stoyan Alexandrov told reporters.

The shareholders' meeting on Saturday also authorised the bank's board to decide on a further capital rise to 25 billion levs in the next five years in line with expected rises of central bank minimum capital requirements.

The CCB's paid-in capital amounted to two billion levs at end-February, up from 1.069 billion levs at end-December after Bulgaria's Bulbank contributed around $1 million worth of dollar-denominated domestic bad debt bonds, Alexandrov said.

The Bulgarian National Bank last week allowed state-owned Bulbank, a co-operative union and a local wine maker to acquire up 35, 28 and 35 percent of CCB voting shares, respectively. The permission also applies to the increased capital.

With the contribution of the bonds Bulbank acquired 34.6 percent of the voting shares. The Central Co-operative Union now holds around 26.4 percent of the voting shares, down from 49.6 percent, and the Gamza wine maker has 28.5 percent.
Bad debt bonds were issued two year ago to cover local banks' unperforming loans extended to state companies before 1991.
The bank's operating profit for the first two months of 1997 totalled 6.3 billion levs, which fully covered its risk assets, Alexandrov said. CCB posted around 6.4 million levs loss last year.
The CCB's provisions rose to 3.3 billion levs on February 28 from 669 million levs at end-1996.
"The bank's operating profit for the first two months of this year resulted from an increase in the number of clients," said Alexandrov.
The number of CCB clients rose by some 2,400 in the first two months of 1997, he added.

CCB's capital to risk assets ratio was 22.8 percent at end-February according to the local accounting standards and 15.9 percent according to international standards, against minus 15.5 percent at end-1996.

The shareholders elected a seven-member board of directors, which includes Dimitar Kostov, a former finance minister in the previous Socialist government, Stoyan Alexandrov, also a former finance minister, and Momchil Andreev, a former executive director of state-owned Bulgarian Post Bank.
